raw_text:
# Sacubitril/Valsartan in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure worldwide [1]. For decades, neurohormonal blockade with renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors, beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists formed the cornerstone of therapy for HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [2]. The introduction of sacubitril/valsartan, a first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), represented a paradigm shift in pharmacotherapy [3].

## Mechanism of Action

Sacubitril/valsartan combines the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril with the angiotensin receptor blocker valsartan in a single supramolecular complex [4]. Neprilysin is an endopeptidase that degrades several vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [5]. By inhibiting neprilysin, the natriuretic peptide system is augmented, promoting natriuresis, vasodilation, and anti-remodeling effects, while valsartan simultaneously blocks the maladaptive effects of angiotensin II [6]. Because neprilysin inhibition raises angiotensin II levels, combining it with an ARB rather than an ACE inhibitor avoids the increased angioedema risk seen with the earlier agent omapatrilat [7].

## Pivotal Clinical Trial Evidence in HFrEF

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial randomized 8442 patients with HFrEF (NYHA class II–IV, ejection fraction ≤40%, later ≤35%) to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril [8]. The trial was stopped early for benefit; sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20%, and reduced all-cause mortality [8]. Subsequent analyses demonstrated reductions in sudden cardiac death and progression of disease [9,10]. The benefits were consistent across subgroups, including the elderly and those with diabetes [11,12]. These results led to rapid incorporation into international guidelines [13].

The TRANSITION and PIONEER-HF trials extended evidence to patients hospitalized with acute decompensated HF [14,15]. PIONEER-HF showed that in-hospital initiation produced a greater reduction in NT-proBNP than enalapril, with a favorable safety profile, supporting earlier initiation rather than waiting for outpatient stabilization [15]. Real-world registries have largely corroborated these findings [16].

## Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction

The PARAGON-HF trial evaluated sacubitril/valsartan against valsartan in 4822 patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF; EF ≥45%) [17]. The primary composite of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death narrowly missed statistical significance (rate ratio 0.87; P=0.06) [17]. However, subgroup analyses suggested benefit in patients with lower ejection fractions and in women [18,19]. A pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF indicated benefit extending into the range of mildly reduced and lower-preserved ejection fraction [20]. These data informed an expanded, though nuanced, regulatory and guideline position for patients with below-normal ejection fraction [21].

## Safety and Tolerability

The principal adverse effects of sacubitril/valsartan are hypotension, hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction, and, rarely, angioedema [8,22]. A 36-hour washout period is required when switching from an ACE inhibitor to mitigate angioedema risk [13]. The drug appears to attenuate the decline in renal function compared with RAS inhibition alone in some analyses [23]. Sacubitril/valsartan also reduces glycated hemoglobin and may delay insulin initiation in diabetic patients [24]. Effects on biomarkers, including reductions in high-sensitivity troponin and improvements in cardiac reverse remodeling, have been documented in mechanistic studies such as PROVE-HF and EVALUATE-HF [25,26].

## Guideline Recommendations and Implementation

Current guidelines recommend ARNI as a preferred RAS-modulating agent in HFrEF, often as part of quadruple "foundational" therapy alongside beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors [21,27]. Cost-effectiveness analyses have generally supported its value despite higher acquisition costs relative to generic ACE inhibitors [28]. Despite robust evidence, implementation remains suboptimal owing to therapeutic inertia, cost, and tolerability concerns, and underutilization persists in real-world practice [29]. Strategies emphasizing early and simultaneous initiation of foundational therapies are increasingly advocated [30].

## Conclusion

Sacubitril/valsartan has transformed the management of HFrEF by demonstrating superiority over conventional RAS inhibition in reducing mortality and hospitalization [8]. Its role in HFpEF is more limited but clinically relevant for patients with below-normal ejection fractions [17,20]. Evidence supporting early in-hospital initiation and its incorporation into combination foundational therapy further solidifies its central place in contemporary HF care [15,30]. Ongoing efforts must focus on improving implementation, addressing cost barriers, and refining patient selection to maximize population-level benefit.
